description: A non-selective beta-blocker with Class III antiarrhythmic potassium channel-blocking properties, used for ventricular arrhythmias and maintaining sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation.
mechanism_of_action: D- and L-isomers block beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors; D-isomer selectively blocks rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), prolonging myocardial action potential duration and effective refractory period.
pharmacodynamics: Slows heart rate, decreases AV nodal conduction velocity, and prolongs ventricular refractory periods; carries high dose-dependent risk of Torsades de pointes.
absorption: Rapidly and completely absorbed (>90%); absorption reduced by 20% by food (especially dairy/calcium).
distribution: Widely distributed; does not cross blood-brain barrier significantly; zero plasma protein binding (0%).
metabolism: Not metabolized by the liver; excreted completely unaltered by the kidneys.
excretion: Excreted entirely unchanged in urine via glomerular filtration (>80-90%).
indications: Maintenance of normal sinus rhythm in patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation or flutter
Treatment of documented life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias (sustained VT)
contraindications: Second- or third-degree AV block without pacemaker
warnings: Black box warning: Must be initiated in a facility with continuous cardiac monitoring and resuscitation capabilities for at least 3 days
Proarrhythmic risk: Torsades de pointes occurs in 2-4% (highest in females, hypokalemia, renal dysfunction)
Dose strictly based on creatinine clearance

Calculate QTc interval before every dose (discontinue if QTc > 500 ms)
Serum potassium and magnesium (maintain K+ > 4.0 mEq/L, Mg2+ > 2.0 mg/dL)
Serum creatinine

description: A non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker with potent intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA), lowering blood pressure with minimal resting bradycardia or metabolic suppression.
mechanism_of_action: Partial agonist at beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity - ISA); competitively blocks catecholamines during exercise/stress while providing low-level basal receptor stimulation at rest.
pharmacodynamics: Reduces peripheral vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure without causing marked resting bradycardia, cardiac depression, or lipid elevation.
absorption: Rapidly and completely absorbed (approx. 90-100%); peak plasma levels in 1 to 2 hours; food has no effect.
distribution: Widely distributed into tissues; crosses blood-brain barrier; 40-50% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Metabolized extensively in the liver (approx. 60-65%) to inactive hydroxylated and glucuronide metabolites.
excretion: Excreted in urine (approx. 35-40% as unchanged parent drug, remainder as metabolites).
indications: Essential hypertension in patients prone to excessive resting bradycardia
Mild to moderate angina pectoris
contraindications: Bronchial asthma or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Severe cardiogenic shock or overt decompensated heart failure
warnings: Avoid abrupt cessation (taper over 1-2 weeks)
May worsen angina or precipitate arrhythmias if withdrawn suddenly
Caution in peripheral vascular disease
monitoring: Blood pressure and resting heart rate
Assessment for sleep disturbances and bronchospasm

description: A phosphinic acid-containing ACE inhibitor prodrug characterized by dual, compensatory hepatic and renal elimination, eliminating the need for dose reductions in renal impairment.
mechanism_of_action: Hydrolyzed in the liver and gastrointestinal mucosa to fosinoprilat, which competitively inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), blocking conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and preventing bradykinin degradation.
pharmacodynamics: Reduces systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure without reflex tachycardia; improves cardiac output in heart failure; demonstrates unique 50:50 compensatory hepatobiliary and renal clearance.

distribution: High protein binding (>99% for fosinoprilat, primarily albumin); low volume of distribution.
metabolism: Rapidly and completely cleaved by mucosal and hepatic esterases to active fosinoprilat; no cytochrome P450 involvement.
excretion: Eliminated equally by hepatic/biliary excretion (approx. 50%) and renal excretion (approx. 50%); in renal failure, biliary clearance increases compensatory up to 100%.

Congestive heart failure (adjunct to diuretics and digitalis)
Proteinuric chronic kidney disease

description: A lipophilic bicyclic prodrug ACE inhibitor with high vascular tissue ACE affinity and endothelial protective actions, used for hypertension and heart failure.
mechanism_of_action: De-esterified in the liver to active quinaprilat, a potent competitive inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE); exhibits extremely high affinity and binding to tissue-bound ACE in vascular endothelium.
pharmacodynamics: Suppresses tissue and circulating angiotensin II, reduces systemic vascular resistance, preserves renal blood flow, and improves arterial compliance and endothelial dysfunction.
absorption: Rapidly absorbed (approx. 60%); peak quinapril in 1 hour; conversion to quinaprilat yields peak levels in 2 hours; high-fat meals reduce absorption by 25-30%.
distribution: Widely distributed into vascular tissue; quinaprilat is 97% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Extensively hydrolyzed in the liver to active quinaprilat and minor inactive diketopiperazine metabolites.
excretion: Excreted in urine (approx. 61%, primarily as quinaprilat) and faeces (approx. 37%).
bioavailability: Approximately 60% absorbed; active quinaprilat bioavailability is 38%
half_life: Parent 1 hour; active quinaprilat effective half-life 3 hours (terminal dissociation half-life 25 hours)

Congestive heart failure (adjunct therapy in NYHA Class II-IV)
Hypertension with vascular endothelial dysfunction
contraindications: History of ACE inhibitor-induced or idiopathic angioedema
Concomitant sacubitril/valsartan or aliskiren in diabetics

Hyperkalemia and first-dose hypotension

mechanism_of_action: Bioactivated in the liver by ester cleavage to trandolaprilat, an exceptionally potent, slow-dissociating competitive inhibitor of ACE with high tissue affinity; blocks angiotensin II formation and promotes bradykinin-mediated vasodilation.

excretion: Excreted in faeces (approx. 66%) via biliary elimination and urine (approx. 33%).

indications: Add-on therapy for the symptomatic treatment of chronic stable angina pectoris in patients inadequately controlled by or intolerant of first-line antianginal therapies
Adjuvant therapy in ischemic cardiomyopathy
contraindications: Parkinson's disease, parkinsonism, tremors, restless legs syndrome, and other movement disorders
warnings: PARKINSONIAN SYMPTOMS: Can cause or aggravate parkinsonian symptoms (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, gait instability), especially in elderly patients; symptoms are usually reversible upon discontinuation
Must be discontinued permanently if movement disorders develop
Not indicated for acute angina attacks
drug_interactions: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic cytochrome P450 interactions reported
Additive CNS effects with dopamine antagonists
monitoring: Regular screening for movement disorders (tremor, slow movements, gait unsteadiness)
Renal function (creatinine clearance) at baseline and annually
Angina attack frequency
pregnancy: Avoid during pregnancy due to limited human safety data.
lactation: Excretion in breast milk unknown; breastfeeding not recommended.
pediatric: Safety and efficacy in children under 18 years not established.
geriatric: Higher risk of drug-induced parkinsonism and falls in senior patients; monitor closely for resting tremor.
renal: Dose reduction required: if CrCl 30-60 mL/min, reduce dose by 50% (give 35 mg MR once daily in the morning); contraindicated if CrCl < 30 mL/min.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment required in hepatic disease.
advantages: Pure metabolic cytoprotective mechanism that optimizes oxygen efficiency without affecting heart rate or blood pressure
Can be combined safely with any hemodynamic antianginal (beta-blockers, CCBs, nitrates)
Reduces myocardial injury during angioplasty and cardiac surgery
disadvantages: Risk of drug-induced Parkinson's symptoms (tremor, gait freezing) in elderly patients
Not approved in the United States (extensively used in Europe, Asia, and India)
key_points: Metabolic heart protector that makes heart muscle use oxygen more efficiently
Stop the medication and inform your doctor immediately if you notice finger tremors or walking stiffness
memory_trick: TRIMETA-zidine: Thiolase (3-KAT) Inhibitor; Metabolic Energy optimizer; Tremor/Parkinson risk.
